For each \(d\in\{2,3\}\), let \(X_{n,d}\) consist of \(n\) independent points uniformly distributed in \([0,1]^d\), using ordinary Euclidean distance without periodic boundary conditions. At parameter \(a\geq0\), define the Čech complex by
\[
\mathcal C_a(X_{n,d})=\left\{\sigma\subseteq X_{n,d}:\bigcap_{x\in\sigma}\overline B(x,\sqrt a)\neq\varnothing\right\},
\]
where \(\overline B(x,r)\) is the closed Euclidean ball of radius \(r\). Compute persistent homology in degree one over the field \(\mathbb F_2\) of two elements. Let \(D_{n,d}\) be the multiset of birth–death pairs \((b,\delta)\) of all positive-length intervals, so \(0<b<\delta<\infty\); zero-length intervals are discarded, multiplicities are retained, and no death-time cutoff is imposed.

Assign to each pair the reduced coordinate
\[
s(b,\delta)=\sqrt{\tfrac12\log(\delta/b)},
\]
with natural logarithms. Writing \(m_{n,d}=|D_{n,d}|\), define the empirical probability measure
\[
\widehat\mu_{n,d}=\frac1{m_{n,d}}\sum_{(b,\delta)\in D_{n,d}}\delta_{s(b,\delta)}
\]
when \(m_{n,d}>0\), where \(\delta_x\) denotes unit point mass at \(x\); when \(m_{n,d}=0\), set \(\widehat\mu_{n,d}=\delta_1\).

You may assume that \(\widehat\mu_{n,d}\) converges weakly in probability to a deterministic probability measure \(\mu_d\) on \([0,\infty)\), meaning that its integrals against bounded continuous functions converge in probability to those of \(\mu_d\). You may also assume that the distribution function \(F_d(t)=\mu_d([0,t])\) has an expansion
\[
F_d(t)=c_dt+q_dt^2+o(t^2)\qquad(t\downarrow0),\qquad c_d>0.
\]
Define
\[
K_d=\frac12+\frac{q_d}{c_d^2},
\]
which is unchanged by multiplying the reduced coordinate by a positive constant, or equivalently by additively centering its logarithm. Determine the exact ordered pair \((K_2,K_3)\).
</problem>

8	The main issue is that a short persistence interval need not, in general, be paired with the longest edge of its death triangle. The proof below controls precisely this issue; ignoring it without an error estimate would not suffice to determine the quadratic coefficient.
9	
10	## 1. Birth edges and the total number of intervals
11	
12	We work with point configurations in general position. All the general-position properties used below hold almost surely for the samples in the question.
13	
14	Call an edge \(e=\{p,q\}\) **Gabriel** if its open diameter ball contains no other sample point. Write
15	\[
16	r_e=\frac{|p-q|}{2}.
17	\]
18	Its Čech birth parameter is \(r_e^2\).
19	
20	Two elementary persistence facts will be useful.
21	
22	**Fact 1.** The edges giving positive-length \(H_1\) intervals are exactly the Gabriel edges other than the \(n-1\) edges that merge components. Consequently, if \(G(X)\) is the number of Gabriel edges,
23	\[
24	m(X)=G(X)-n+1. \tag{1}
25	\]
26	
27	Indeed, if \(e\) is not Gabriel, a point inside its diameter ball gives a triangle appearing at the same time as \(e\), with both other edges strictly shorter. Thus \(e\) is paired at length zero. If \(e\) is Gabriel, no triangle containing it appears at its birth, so it either merges components or creates a positive-length \(H_1\) class. Eventually the complex is a simplex, so all the latter classes die.
28	
29	**Fact 2.** Suppose the first triangle containing an edge \(e\) has \(e\) as its longest edge. Then that triangle is paired with \(e\).
30	
31	To see this directly by boundary-matrix reduction, order edges by their birth times. The triangle boundary has largest edge \(e\), and no earlier triangle column contains \(e\). Therefore its pivot is \(e\).
32	
33	Both statements concern ordinary Čech persistence, not an approximation by a graph or a different filtration.
34	
35	## 2. A geometric count of short intervals
36	
37	It is convenient to replace \(t\) by
38	\[
39	u=\sqrt{e^{2t^2}-1}.
40	\]
41	Then
42	\[
43	s(b,\delta)\le t
44	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
45	\delta\le b(1+u^2),
46	\qquad
47	u=\sqrt2\,t+O(t^3). \tag{2}
48	\]
49	
50	Fix a Gabriel edge, and translate and rotate its endpoints to
51	\[
52	p=(-r,0),\qquad q=(r,0),
53	\]
54	where the second coordinate belongs to \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Write another point as \(z=(x,y)\), with \(\rho=|y|\).
55	
56	The circumcenter of \(p,q,z\), in their affine plane, is at perpendicular distance
57	\[
58	h=\frac{x^2+\rho^2-r^2}{2\rho}
59	\]
60	from the edge midpoint. Since the diameter ball is empty, \(h>0\).
61	
62	Define
63	\[
64	U_{r,u}=\left\{(x,y):x^2+|y|^2\le r^2+2ur|y|\right\}. \tag{3}
65	\]
66	A point in \(U_{r,u}\) outside the diameter ball gives a triangle whose circumradius is at most \(r\sqrt{1+u^2}\). In particular, its Čech parameter is at most \(r^2(1+u^2)\).
67	
68	Let:
69	
70	* \(A_X(u)\) be the number of positive intervals with \(\delta/b\le1+u^2\);
71	* \(H_X(u)\) be the number of Gabriel edges having another point in \(U_{r,u}\);
72	* \(B_X(u)\) be the number of Gabriel edges \(e\) for which some triangle containing \(e\)
73	  1. has Čech parameter at most \(r_e^2(1+u^2)\), and
74	  2. has another edge at least as long as \(e\).
75	
76	Then
77	\[
78	\boxed{\quad |A_X(u)-H_X(u)|\le B_X(u).\quad} \tag{4}
79	\]
80	
81	Here is why this bound handles arbitrary persistence pairings. A death of the class born at \(e\) requires some triangle containing \(e\) to have appeared by that time: otherwise every triangle boundary, and every linear combination of such boundaries, has zero coefficient on \(e\).
82	
83	If \(e\) is not counted by \(B_X(u)\), every triangle containing it that appears by the specified time has \(e\) as its longest edge. By Fact 2, the first such triangle pairs with \(e\). Moreover, such a triangle is acute, and its circumradius satisfies the bound exactly when its third vertex belongs to (3). Thus, outside the exceptional edges counted by \(B_X(u)\), the two counts agree.
84	
85	### The exceptional count is higher order
86	
87	For \(0<u\le1/4\), the possible third vertices of a triangle counted in \(B_X(u)\) occupy volume
88	\[
89	O\!\left(r^d u^{d+1}\right). \tag{5}
90	\]
91	
92	We give explicit bounds. Suppose a ball of radius \(R=r\sqrt{1+u^2}\), centered at \(c\), contains \(p,q,z\), and suppose \(|z-p|\ge2r\). Containment of \(p,q\) gives
93	\[
94	|c|^2+2r|c_1|\le r^2u^2.
95	\]
96	Thus
97	\[
98	|c|\le ru,\qquad |c_1|\le \frac{ru^2}{2}.
99	\]
100	The parallelogram identity gives
101	\[
102	\left|\frac{z+p}{2}-c\right|^2
103	=\frac{|z-c|^2+|p-c|^2}{2}-\frac{|z-p|^2}{4}
104	\le r^2u^2.
105	\]
106	Since \(p=-q\), it follows that
107	\[
108	|z-q|\le4ru.
109	\]
110	In particular, \(\rho\le4ru\). Combining this with \(|z-p|\ge2r\), and using \(u\le1/4\), gives
111	\[
112	r-8ru^2\le x\le r+ru^2.
113	\]
114	So \(z\) lies in a cylinder of longitudinal width \(9ru^2\) and transverse radius \(4ru\), near one endpoint. There is an analogous cylinder near the other endpoint. Their total volume is at most
115	\[
116	C_d r^d u^{d+1},
117	\qquad
118	C_d=18\,4^{d-1}\kappa_{d-1}, \tag{6}
119	\]
120	where \(\kappa_j\) denotes the unit \(j\)-ball volume.
121	
122	In dimensions two and three, therefore, this error cannot affect a quadratic expansion in \(u\).
123	
124	## 3. The limiting local counts
125	
126	Rescale the cube to volume \(n\), so the sample has asymptotic intensity one. This scaling does not change any persistence ratio.
127	
128	We use the following elementary local-count law of large numbers.
129	
130	**Local-count lemma.** For the counts \(G,H(u),B(u)\), normalized by \(n\), their expectations converge to their unit-intensity Poisson expectations per unit volume. For \(G\) and \(H(u)\), convergence also holds in probability.
131	
132	For completeness, this applies to the nonperiodic binomial samples here for the following reasons.
133	
134	1. Truncate to edges with \(r_e\le L\). Each edge event is then determined by points within a fixed distance of an endpoint. Its score is bounded by a polynomial in the number of points in a fixed-radius ball.
135	2. Away from the boundary, the local binomial point process converges to a unit Poisson process, with uniformly bounded moments of all these local point counts.
136	3. For two disjoint, bounded neighborhoods, their joint binomial restrictions converge to independent Poisson restrictions. In the variance of the normalized count, nearby pairs occupy an \(O(1/n)\) fraction, while distant-pair covariances tend to zero. Boundary neighborhoods occupy an \(o(1)\) fraction. Thus each fixed-\(L\) count satisfies the claimed law of large numbers.
137	4. The truncation is harmless uniformly in \(n\). A diameter ball of radius \(r\), centered in the cube, has intersection with the cube of volume at least \(c_dr^d\). Its emptiness probability is therefore at most \(e^{-c'_dr^d}\). Summing over edges bounds discarded expectations by a constant times
138	   \[
139	   \int_L^\infty r^{d-1}e^{-c'_dr^d}\,dr.
140	   \]
141	   For the exceptional count, summing over possible third vertices adds only a factor \(O(r^d)\), which is still integrable.
142	
143	These arguments also prove convergence of the exceptional-count expectations, which is all we need for \(B\).
144	
145	Now compute the Poisson expectations. Put
146	\[
147	L_d=2^{d-1}.
148	\]
149	For an unordered edge, write its displacement length as \(2r\). The probability that its diameter ball is empty is \(e^{-\kappa_dr^d}\). Hence the Gabriel-edge intensity is
150	\[
151	\begin{aligned}
152	g_d
153	&=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}
154	 e^{-\kappa_d(|z|/2)^d}\,dz\\
155	&=2^{d-1}d\kappa_d\int_0^\infty
156	r^{d-1}e^{-\kappa_dr^d}\,dr
157	=L_d.
158	\end{aligned} \tag{7}
159	\]
160	By (1),
161	\[
162	\frac{m_{n,d}}n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}M_d:=L_d-1.
163	\tag{8}
164	\]
165	In particular,
166	\[
167	M_2=1,\qquad M_3=3.
168	\]
169	
170	Let
171	\[
172	V_d(u)=\operatorname{vol}(U_{1,u}).
173	\]
174	The diameter ball is contained in \(U_{r,u}\). For a Poisson process, emptiness of that ball and presence of a point in its outer part are independent events. Thus the limiting intensity of \(H(u)\) is
175	\[
176	\begin{aligned}
177	h_d(u)
178	&=L_dd\kappa_d\int_0^\infty r^{d-1}
179	\left(e^{-\kappa_dr^d}-e^{-V_d(u)r^d}\right)\,dr\\
180	&=\boxed{\displaystyle L_d\left(1-\frac{\kappa_d}{V_d(u)}\right).}
181	\end{aligned} \tag{9}
182	\]
183	
184	The same edge integral, using (6) and a union bound over third points, bounds the exceptional intensity by
185	\[
186	\begin{aligned}
187	\beta_d(u)
188	&\le L_dd\kappa_d C_du^{d+1}
189	  \int_0^\infty r^{2d-1}e^{-\kappa_dr^d}\,dr\\
190	&=\frac{L_dC_d}{\kappa_d}u^{d+1}.
191	\end{aligned} \tag{10}
192	\]
193	
194	## 4. Transfer to the assumed limiting persistence measure
195	
196	At every continuity point \(t\) of \(F_d\), the assumed weak convergence in probability implies convergence of the empirical distribution functions. Together with (8), this gives
197	\[
198	\frac{A_{X_{n,d}}(u(t))}{n}
199	\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}M_dF_d(t).
200	\]
201	On the other hand,
202	\[
203	\frac{H_{X_{n,d}}(u)}n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}h_d(u).
204	\]
205	
206	Apply (4), and then the expectation bound (10). For example, taking an almost surely convergent subsequence and applying Fatou's lemma yields
207	\[
208	\left|M_dF_d(t)-h_d(u(t))\right|
209	\le \beta_d(u(t)).
210	\]
211	Continuity points are dense, and right continuity extends this bound to all \(t\). Consequently,
212	\[
213	\boxed{\displaystyle
214	F_d(t)=\frac{h_d(u(t))}{M_d}+O(t^{d+1}).}
215	\tag{11}
216	\]
217	This is the step ensuring that nonlocal or otherwise non-obvious persistence pairings do not change the coefficients being computed.
218	
219	## 5. Volume expansion and the constants
220	
221	In spherical coordinates around the edge direction, let \(\theta\) be the polar angle. The radial boundary of \(U_{1,u}\) is
222	\[
223	R_u(\theta)=u\sin\theta+\sqrt{1+u^2\sin^2\theta}.
224	\]
225	Therefore
226	\[
227	\frac{R_u(\theta)^d}{d}
228	=\frac1d+u\sin\theta+\frac d2u^2\sin^2\theta+O(u^3).
229	\]
230	
231	Integrating over the sphere gives
232	\[
233	\begin{aligned}
234	V_2(u)&=\pi+4u+\pi u^2+O(u^3),\\
235	V_3(u)&=\frac{4\pi}{3}+\pi^2u+4\pi u^2+O(u^3).
236	\end{aligned} \tag{12}
237	\]
238	
239	Write
240	\[
241	\frac{V_d(u)}{\kappa_d}=1+a_du+b_du^2+O(u^3).
242	\]
243	The values are
244	\[
245	(a_2,b_2)=\left(\frac4\pi,1\right),
246	\qquad
247	(a_3,b_3)=\left(\frac{3\pi}{4},3\right).
248	\]
249	Equations (9) and (11), with \(u=\sqrt2\,t+O(t^3)\), give
250	\[
251	c_d=\frac{\sqrt2\,L_da_d}{M_d},
252	\qquad
253	q_d=\frac{2L_d(b_d-a_d^2)}{M_d}.
254	\]
255	Explicitly,
256	\[
257	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
258	d&c_d&q_d\\ \hline
259	2&\displaystyle\frac{8\sqrt2}{\pi}
260	 &\displaystyle4-\frac{64}{\pi^2}\\[2mm]
261	3&\displaystyle\sqrt2\,\pi
262	 &\displaystyle8-\frac{3\pi^2}{2}.
263	\end{array}
264	\]
265	
266	It follows that
267	\[
268	K_2=\frac12+
269	\frac{4-64/\pi^2}{128/\pi^2}
270	=\frac{\pi^2}{32},
271	\]
272	and
273	\[
274	K_3=\frac12+
275	\frac{8-3\pi^2/2}{2\pi^2}
276	=\frac4{\pi^2}-\frac14.
277	\]
278	
279	## 6. Executed Python checks
280	
281	The following code does more than print the proposed constants. It:
282	
283	* symbolically derives the radial and volume expansions;
284	* computes \(c_d,q_d,K_d\);
285	* independently checks the Poisson integral by numerical quadrature;
286	* constructs actual finite Čech \(H_1\) persistence by \(\mathbb F_2\) triangle-boundary reduction;
287	* checks the exact interval-count identity (1);
288	* checks the deterministic comparison (4).
289	
290	Only vertices, edges, and triangles are needed to compute \(H_1\). The numerical random tests are checks of the proof's finite identities, not substitutes for the arguments above.
